title: Organisms and Populations
description: Grade 12 Biology: organisms and their environment, adaptations to abiotic factors, population attributes and growth, and population interactions like predation and competition.

topics.title: Organisms and Their Environment
topics.concept:
Ecology is the study of how organisms interact with one another and with their surroundings. The place where an organism lives is its habitat, and everything around it makes up its environment. The environment has two kinds of components: abiotic (non-living) factors — such as temperature, water, light and soil — and biotic (living) factors — other organisms like predators, prey, competitors and parasites.

Organisms must cope with their abiotic conditions, and over time they develop adaptations — special features that help them survive and reproduce in their habitat. Some examples:

  • Desert plants (like cactus) have thick stems to store water, spines instead of leaves, and a thick waxy surface to reduce water loss.
  • Desert animals (like the kangaroo rat) can survive on very little water and stay in burrows during the day.
  • Polar animals have thick fur or fat to keep warm; small ears and limbs reduce heat loss.
  • Some animals migrate or go into a resting state to escape harsh seasons — hibernation (winter sleep) and aestivation (summer dormancy).

Where an organism cannot change its surroundings, it adjusts its own body (physiology) or behaviour to manage. These adaptations show how living things are wonderfully matched to their environment.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is the difference between abiotic and biotic factors?
examples.solution:
One is non-living, one is living.

  • Abiotic: non-living factors (temperature, water, light, soil).
  • Biotic: living factors (predators, prey, competitors).
examples.answer: Abiotic factors are non-living (temperature, water, light, soil); biotic factors are living (other organisms).

examples.problem: Example 2: Give two adaptations of a desert plant like the cactus.
examples.solution:
Deserts are hot and dry.

  • Thick stem to store water; spines instead of leaves.
  • Thick waxy surface to reduce water loss.
examples.answer: A cactus has a thick water-storing stem, spines instead of leaves, and a waxy surface to reduce water loss.

examples.solution:
It helps escape harsh seasons.

  • Hibernation is a resting (dormant) state in which some animals pass the cold winter.
examples.answer: Hibernation is a winter sleep/dormant state by which some animals survive the cold season.

recap:
• Ecology = study of organisms and their interactions with surroundings; habitat + environment.
  • Environment: abiotic (temperature, water, light, soil) + biotic (predators, prey, competitors).
  • Adaptations: desert plants (water-storing stem, spines, waxy), polar animals (fur/fat), hibernation/aestivation.

quiz.q: Temperature, water and soil are examples of ____ factors.
quiz.explanation: Non-living factors like temperature and soil are abiotic.

quiz.q: A cactus has spines instead of leaves mainly to:
quiz.explanation: Spines reduce surface area, cutting water loss in the desert.

topics.title: Population Attributes and Growth
topics.concept:
Organisms of the same species living together in a particular area form a population. Studying populations helps us understand how species survive, grow and decline. A population has several measurable attributes that an individual does not:

  • Population density — the number of individuals per unit area (or volume).
  • Birth rate (natality) and death rate (mortality) — the rate at which individuals are born and die.
  • Sex ratio — the proportion of males to females.
  • Age structure — the proportion of individuals of different ages (young, adult, old), often shown as an age pyramid, which can predict whether a population will grow, stay stable or decline.

Populations change in size through births and immigration (which add individuals) and deaths and emigration (which remove them). When food and space are unlimited, a population can grow very fast in a J-shaped (exponential) curve. But in nature, resources are limited; the largest population an environment can support is its carrying capacity (K). As the population nears K, growth slows and levels off, giving an S-shaped (sigmoid / logistic) curve. The S-shaped curve is more realistic because no environment has unlimited resources.

examples.solution:
It is a group of one species.

  • A population is a group of organisms of the same species living together in a particular area.
examples.answer: A population is a group of organisms of the same species living together in a given area.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name two attributes of a population.
examples.solution:
These apply to groups, not individuals.

  • Population density and birth/death rates (also sex ratio, age structure).
examples.answer: Population density and birth/death rates (also sex ratio and age structure).

examples.solution:
It is a limit set by resources.

  • Carrying capacity (K) is the largest population an environment can support with its resources.
examples.answer: Carrying capacity (K) is the maximum population size an environment can support with its available resources.

recap:
• Population = same species in an area; attributes: density, natality/mortality, sex ratio, age structure (age pyramid).
  • Size changes by births + immigration (add) vs deaths + emigration (remove).
  • Unlimited resources → J-shaped (exponential); limited → S-shaped (logistic) levelling at carrying capacity (K).

quiz.q: The number of individuals per unit area is the population's:
quiz.explanation: Population density is individuals per unit area.

quiz.q: The maximum population an environment can support is its:
quiz.explanation: Carrying capacity (K) is the maximum the environment can support.

topics.title: Population Interactions
topics.concept:
No species lives alone; populations interact with one another in many ways. These population interactions can help or harm the species involved:

  • Predation — one organism (the predator) kills and eats another (the prey), e.g. a lion eating a deer. Predators control prey numbers and keep ecosystems balanced. (Herbivores eating plants are like predators of plants.)
  • Competition — two organisms struggle for the same limited resource (food, space, light), e.g. two plants competing for sunlight. Both are harmed.
  • Parasitism — one organism (the parasite) lives on or in another (the host) and harms it, e.g. ticks on a dog, or tapeworm in humans. The parasite benefits, the host is harmed.
  • Mutualism — both species benefit, e.g. bees and flowers (bees get nectar, flowers get pollinated), or lichens (an alga and a fungus living together).
  • Commensalism — one benefits and the other is unaffected, e.g. an orchid growing on a tree branch for support.

A useful way to summarise these is by who is helped (+), harmed (−) or unaffected (0): predation and parasitism are (+ −), competition is (− −), mutualism is (+ +), and commensalism is (+ 0). These interactions weave organisms into the web of life and keep nature in balance.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is predation? Give an example.
examples.solution:
One organism eats another.

  • Predation is when a predator kills and eats prey.
  • Example: a lion eating a deer.
examples.answer: Predation is when one organism (predator) kills and eats another (prey), e.g. a lion eating a deer.

examples.problem: Example 2: Give an example of mutualism and say why it is mutualistic.
examples.solution:
Both partners benefit.

  • Bees and flowers: bees get nectar, flowers get pollinated.
  • Both benefit, so it is mutualism.
examples.answer: Bees and flowers — bees get nectar and flowers get pollinated, so both benefit (mutualism).

examples.problem: Example 3: In parasitism, who benefits and who is harmed?
examples.solution:
One gains at the other's cost.

  • The parasite benefits; the host is harmed.
examples.answer: The parasite benefits and the host is harmed.

recap:
• Predation (+−): predator kills prey (lion–deer); controls numbers.
  • Competition (−−): struggle for the same resource.
  • Parasitism (+−): parasite benefits, host harmed (tick, tapeworm).
  • Mutualism (++): both benefit (bee–flower, lichen); commensalism (+0): one benefits, other unaffected (orchid on tree).

quiz.q: A relationship in which both species benefit is:
quiz.explanation: In mutualism both partners benefit (e.g. bee and flower).

quiz.q: A tapeworm living in a human is an example of:
quiz.explanation: The parasite benefits while harming the host — parasitism.

questions.q: The study of organisms and their interactions with the environment is:
questions.explanation: Ecology studies organisms and their environment.

questions.q: The place where an organism lives is its:
questions.explanation: The habitat is where an organism lives.

questions.q: Temperature, light and soil are ____ factors.
questions.explanation: These non-living factors are abiotic.

questions.q: Spines and a thick waxy stem in a cactus help it to:
questions.explanation: These adaptations reduce water loss in the desert.

questions.q: Winter sleep by which some animals escape the cold is:
questions.explanation: Hibernation is winter dormancy.

questions.q: A group of organisms of the same species in an area is a:
questions.explanation: A population is one species in an area.

questions.q: The number of individuals per unit area is the:
questions.explanation: Population density is individuals per unit area.

questions.q: The proportion of young, adult and old individuals is the:
questions.explanation: Age structure shows the proportion of different ages.

questions.q: Unlimited resources produce a ____ growth curve.
questions.explanation: Exponential growth gives a J-shaped curve.

questions.q: The maximum population an environment can support is its:
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity (K) is the environmental limit.

questions.q: A more realistic, S-shaped population curve is called:
questions.explanation: Limited resources give the logistic (S-shaped) curve.

questions.q: A lion eating a deer is an example of:
questions.explanation: A predator killing and eating prey is predation.

questions.q: Two plants struggling for the same sunlight show:
questions.explanation: Struggle for the same resource is competition.

questions.q: Bees and flowers, where both benefit, show:
questions.explanation: Both benefit, so it is mutualism.

questions.q: An orchid growing on a tree for support (tree unaffected) is:
questions.explanation: One benefits, the other is unaffected — commensalism.

questions.q: A J-shaped growth curve cannot continue forever in nature because:
questions.explanation: Finite food and space eventually slow growth, bending the curve into an S-shape at K.

questions.q: Removing all predators from an area can harm the ecosystem because the prey may:
questions.explanation: Without predation, prey numbers can explode beyond carrying capacity and crash, destabilising the system.

questions.q: An age pyramid with a very broad base (many young) suggests the population will likely:
questions.explanation: A large young cohort will mature and reproduce, so the population is poised to grow.

questions.q: Lichens (alga + fungus) are mutualistic because the alga makes food while the fungus:
questions.explanation: Each partner supplies what the other lacks, so both benefit — true mutualism.

questions.q: A desert kangaroo rat surviving with very little drinking water shows an adaptation to a key ____ factor.
questions.explanation: Coping with scarce water is an adaptation to an abiotic condition of the desert.

questions.q: Both competition and parasitism harm at least one partner, but they differ because in competition:
options: Both organisms are harmed by sharing a resource
questions.explanation: Competition harms both (−−), whereas parasitism helps one and harms the other (+−).
